region: Oceania and the East Asian rim (Japan, Ryukyu, Korea, Taiwan, Hainan, Manchuria/Amur, Polynesia, New Zealand, Australia, Melanesia, Micronesia), 1400–1900

polities.name: Ashikaga shogunate
polities.note: Nominal government of all Japan; after the Ōnin War (1467–77) its effective control shrank to the capital region (Yamashiro and parts of the Kinai). Extent = effective Kinai core in the Sengoku period. Ended when Oda Nobunaga expelled Ashikaga Yoshiaki 1573.

polities.name: Kamakura / Koga kubō
polities.note: Ashikaga branch governing the Kantō; moved to Koga after 1455; reduced to a Hōjō puppet by the 1550s.

polities.name: Yamanouchi Uesugi (Kantō kanrei)
polities.note: Deputies of the Kamakura kubō; held Kōzuke, Musashi and Izu; driven out of Kōzuke by the Later Hōjō 1552 and passed the title to Nagao Kagetora (Uesugi Kenshin).

polities.name: Oda clan
polities.note: Deputy shugo of Owari; Nobunaga unified Owari 1559, took Mino 1567, entered Kyoto 1568; at his death (1582) held central Honshu from Echizen/Kaga to Harima and Kai/Shinano.

polities.name: Toyotomi regime
polities.note: Hideyoshi's hegemony: Shikoku 1585, Kyushu 1587, Kantō and Tōhoku 1590 (all Japan except Ezo). Daimyo kept domains as vassals. Effective rule ended at Sekigahara 1600; Toyotomi house survived at Osaka to 1615.

polities.name: Tokugawa shogunate
polities.note: Overlord of ~270 domains (han) across Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, with Matsumae on southern Ezo; domains listed here (Satsuma, Sendai, Chōshū etc.) sit under it. Direct rule of eastern Ezo 1799–1821 and 1855–68.

polities.name: Empire of Japan
polities.note: Meiji state; annexed Ezo (Hokkaido) 1869, Ryukyu 1879, Kurils 1875, Taiwan 1895, Karafuto 1905, Korea 1910.

polities.name: Takeda clan
polities.note: Shugo of Kai; Shingen conquered Shinano 1541–1553, western Kōzuke and Suruga 1568–69; destroyed by Oda–Tokugawa 1582.

polities.name: Nagao–Uesugi of Echigo
polities.note: Echigo shugo (Uesugi) with Nagao deputies; Nagao Kagetora took the Uesugi name 1561 (Kenshin), adding Etchū and Noto 1576–77. Moved to Aizu 1598 and reduced to Yonezawa Domain 1601–1871.

polities.name: Later Hōjō clan
polities.note: Founded by Ise Sōzui (Hōjō Sōun) in Izu 1493/95; took Odawara 1495; dominated the Kantō by 1560s; destroyed by Hideyoshi's siege of Odawara 1590.

polities.name: Mōri clan
polities.note: Aki kokujin; Motonari overthrew the Ōuchi (1555–57) and Amago (1566) to rule ten western provinces; reduced after Sekigahara to Nagato and Suō (Chōshū/Hagi Domain) 1600–1871.

polities.name: Ōuchi clan
polities.note: Shugo of Suō, Nagato, Buzen and Chikuzen (and Aki/Iwami at times); controlled the Ming tally trade; collapsed after Sue Harukata's coup 1551 and Mōri conquest 1557.

polities.name: Amago clan
polities.note: Deputy shugo of Izumo for the Kyōgoku; independent from c.1486 under Amago Tsunehisa; peak 1530s–50s over eleven San'in/San'yō provinces; fell to the Mōri 1566.

polities.name: Ōtomo clan
polities.note: Shugo of Bungo; under Ōtomo Sōrin (1550–78) held six northern Kyushu provinces; broken by the Shimazu at Mimikawa 1578, saved by Hideyoshi 1587, dispossessed 1593.

polities.name: Shimazu clan
polities.note: Shugo of Satsuma, Ōsumi and Hyūga; unified southern Kyushu by 1570s and nearly all Kyushu 1584–86; submitted to Hideyoshi 1587; Satsuma Domain under the Tokugawa; overlord of Ryukyu from 1609 and annexed Amami 1611.

polities.name: Date clan
polities.note: Southern Mutsu/Dewa lords; Masamune briefly held most of southern Tōhoku 1589 (Aizu); after 1591 based at Iwadeyama, then Sendai Domain (620,000 koku) 1603–1871.

polities.name: Imagawa clan
polities.note: Shugo of Suruga and Tōtōmi; added Mikawa under Yoshimoto (1540s–60); collapsed after Okehazama 1560; Takeda/Tokugawa partition 1568–69.

polities.name: Chōsokabe clan
polities.note: Tosa kokujin; Motochika unified Tosa 1575 and nearly all Shikoku by 1585; reduced to Tosa by Hideyoshi 1585; dispossessed after Sekigahara 1600.

polities.name: Asakura clan
polities.note: Seized Echizen from the Shiba shugo after the Ōnin War; destroyed by Oda Nobunaga 1573.

polities.name: Azai clan
polities.note: Northern Ōmi lords; broke from the Rokkaku; destroyed by Nobunaga 1573.

polities.name: Rokkaku clan
polities.note: Shugo of southern Ōmi; driven out by Nobunaga 1568.

polities.name: Saitō clan of Mino
polities.note: Saitō Dōsan ousted the Toki shugo of Mino 1542; Nobunaga took Inabayama (renamed Gifu) 1567.

polities.name: Toki clan of Mino
polities.note: Shugo of Mino until overthrown by Saitō Dōsan 1542.

polities.name: Tokugawa (Matsudaira) clan before 1603
polities.note: Mikawa kokujin, Imagawa vassals until 1560; Ieyasu held Mikawa and Tōtōmi, five provinces 1582, then the Kantō from 1590 (Edo) before founding the shogunate.

polities.name: Miyoshi clan
polities.note: Awa-based deputies of the Hosokawa; Miyoshi Nagayoshi dominated the Kinai and Awa/Sanuki 1549–64; broken by Nobunaga 1568–73 (Awa branch to 1582).

polities.name: Hosokawa clan (kanrei)
polities.note: Shogunal deputy (kanrei) house holding Settsu, Tanba, Sanuki, Tosa and Awa (Shikoku branch); real power behind the shogunate after 1493 until displaced by Miyoshi Nagayoshi 1549.

polities.name: Satake clan
polities.note: Shugo of Hitachi (seat Ōta, then Mito 1590); transferred to Kubota (Akita) 1602–1871.

polities.name: Mogami clan
polities.note: Dewa lords; under Mogami Yoshiaki held most of Dewa (570,000 koku 1600); attainted 1622.

polities.name: Nanbu clan
polities.note: Northern Mutsu lords; drove the Andō from Tsugaru 1432; lost Tsugaru to Ōura (Tsugaru) Tamenobu 1571–90; Morioka Domain 1599–1871.

polities.name: Tsugaru clan
polities.note: Ōura Tamenobu seized Tsugaru from the Nanbu 1571–90; Hirosaki Domain to 1871.

polities.name: Andō clan
polities.note: 'Ezo kanrei' lords of Tsugaru controlling the Ezo trade and the Wajin footholds on southern Hokkaido; driven out of Tosaminato by the Nanbu 1432/1443; re-established in northern Dewa (Hiyama, Minato) as the Akita clan; moved to Hitachi 1602.

polities.name: Ashina clan
polities.note: Lords of Aizu; destroyed by Date Masamune at Suriagehara 1589.

polities.name: Ryūzōji clan
polities.note: Hizen lords; Ryūzōji Takanobu dominated northwest Kyushu 1570s–1584 (killed at Okitanawate); power passed to the Nabeshima (Saga Domain).

polities.name: Kaga Ikkō-ikki
polities.note: Jōdo Shinshū league that overthrew the Togashi shugo of Kaga 1488 and governed the province until Oda general Shibata Katsuie's conquest 1580; allied with Ishiyama Hongan-ji.

polities.name: Ishiyama Hongan-ji
polities.note: Fortified temple-town headquarters of the Ikkō sect with its own jinaimachi and lands; besieged by Nobunaga 1570–80.

polities.name: Ukita clan
polities.note: Ukita Naoie supplanted the Urakami in Bizen/Mimasaka; Hideie held 570,000 koku under Hideyoshi; dispossessed after Sekigahara.

polities.name: Itō clan of Hyūga
polities.note: Held central/northern Hyūga from Tonokōri; driven out by the Shimazu 1577; restored at Obi Domain 1587–1871 (small).

polities.name: Kikuchi clan
polities.note: Shugo of Higo; declined from the late 15th c.; the line ended 1550 and Higo passed under Ōtomo influence, then Sagara/Shimazu.

polities.name: Sagara clan
polities.note: Lords of southern Higo (Kuma and Ashikita); Hitoyoshi Domain under the Tokugawa.

polities.name: Sō clan
polities.note: Lords of Tsushima managing Japan's relations and trade with Joseon (Busan Waegwan); vassals of the Ashikaga, Toyotomi and Tokugawa.

polities.name: Kōno clan
polities.note: Shugo of Iyo; increasingly dependent on the Mōri; ended with Hideyoshi's Shikoku campaign 1585.

polities.name: Noto Hatakeyama clan
polities.note: Shugo of Noto; Nanao fell to Uesugi Kenshin 1577.

polities.name: Kitabatake clan
polities.note: Hereditary governors (kokushi) of southern Ise; absorbed by Oda Nobunaga (adoption of Nobukatsu 1569, extermination 1576).

polities.name: Satomi clan
polities.note: Lords of Awa province (southern Bōsō peninsula) and, at times, Kazusa; rivals of the Later Hōjō; attainted 1614.

polities.name: Ainu of Hokkaido (all groups)
polities.note: Umbrella entry for the Ainu kotan territories of Hokkaido outside the Wajin enclave; use the regional Ainu groupings below to subdivide. Increasingly under Matsumae trade control after Shakushain's revolt (1669) and the Menashi–Kunashir rebellion (1789); annexed as Hokkaido 1869.

polities.name: Western (Shiribeshi) Ainu
polities.note: Ainu kotan of the southwestern peninsula and Japan Sea coast outside the Wajinchi; boundaries approximate.

polities.name: Ishikari Ainu
polities.note: Ainu of the Ishikari basin (incl. Kamikawa); under chief Haukase they stayed neutral in Shakushain's revolt 1669.

polities.name: Shumkuru (Saru Ainu)
polities.note: Western Hidaka/Iburi Ainu grouping led by Onibishi in the feud with Shakushain's Menashikuru (1648–68).

polities.name: Menashikuru (Shibuchari Ainu)
polities.note: Eastern Hidaka Ainu led by Shakushain, who raised the 1669 revolt against Matsumae; defeated 1669–72.

polities.name: Tokachi Ainu
polities.note: Ainu of the Tokachi plain; boundaries approximate.

polities.name: Eastern Ainu (Kushiro–Akkeshi–Nemuro–Kunashir)
polities.note: Eastern Ainu under chiefs such as Ikotoi of Akkeshi and Tsukinoe of Kunashir; Menashi–Kunashir rebellion 1789; under direct shogunal rule from 1799.

polities.name: Northern (Sōya–Okhotsk) Ainu
polities.note: Ainu of the Sōya strait and Okhotsk coast; boundaries approximate.

polities.name: Sakhalin Ainu
polities.note: Ainu of southern Sakhalin; tributary in the Santan trade to Ming (Nurgan) and Qing; Matsumae trading posts from 1790; Sakhalin ceded to Russia 1875.

polities.name: Kuril Ainu
polities.note: Ainu of the central and northern Kurils (Iturup northward); Russian tribute from the 1700s; Kurils divided 1855 and all ceded to Japan 1875.

polities.name: Matsumae clan
polities.note: Kakizaki deputies of the Andō moved to Matsumae 1514; recognised by Hideyoshi 1590 and Ieyasu 1604 with a monopoly on Ainu trade. Governed the Wajinchi enclave on the Oshima peninsula; Ainu lands beyond were trade fiefs. Domain moved to Yanagawa 1807–21 while the shogunate ruled Ezo directly.

polities.name: Republic of Ezo
polities.note: Tokugawa loyalist state in southern Hokkaido during the Boshin War; surrendered June 1869.

polities.name: Joseon
polities.note: Tributary of Ming and (from 1637) Qing. Northern frontier fixed on the Yalu–Tumen line by the Four Commanderies (1443) and Six Garrisons (1449). Became the Korean Empire 1897.

polities.name: Korean Empire
polities.note: Successor of Joseon; Japanese protectorate 1905, annexed 1910.

polities.name: Hokuzan
polities.note: Northern Okinawa kingdom of the Sanzan period; conquered by Chūzan (Shō Hashi) 1416.

polities.name: Chūzan
polities.note: Central Okinawa kingdom; Shō Hashi conquered Hokuzan 1416 and Nanzan 1429, founding the unified Ryukyu Kingdom. Seat Urasoe, moved to Shuri c.1406.

polities.name: Nanzan
polities.note: Southern Okinawa kingdom; absorbed by Chūzan 1429.

polities.name: Ryukyu Kingdom
polities.note: Unified by Shō Hashi 1429; took Amami 1466 and the Sakishima (Miyako, Yaeyama) by 1500; invaded by Satsuma 1609 and lost Amami (1611) while remaining a Ming/Qing tributary; annexed by Japan as Okinawa Prefecture 1879.

polities.name: Yaeyama chiefdoms
polities.note: Local chiefs (aji) of the Yaeyama Islands; Oyake Akahachi's resistance was crushed by Ryukyu 1500. Miyako's Nakasone Tuyumya sided with Shuri.

polities.name: Amami chiefdoms
polities.note: Local aji of Amami Ōshima, Kikai, Tokunoshima and Okinoerabu before Ryukyu conquest (Kikai 1466); placed under Satsuma 1611.

polities.name: Kingdom of Middag
polities.note: Supra-village polity of the Papora/Babuza/Pazeh plains peoples of west-central Taiwan (western Taichung, northern Changhua); 27 villages at its height, 17 in the 1640s. Submitted to the Dutch 1645; harshly exploited under Tungning; supra-tribal leadership ended after the 1731–32 Dajia-xi uprising was crushed by the Qing. Start date approximate.

polities.name: Dutch Formosa
polities.note: VOC colony around Tainan; controlled the southwestern plains villages and, after expelling the Spanish 1642, the north coast; ousted by Koxinga 1662.

polities.name: Spanish Formosa
polities.note: Spanish outposts at Keelung and Tamsui; expelled by the Dutch 1642.

polities.name: Kingdom of Tungning
polities.note: Ming loyalist Zheng state founded by Koxinga; held the western plains of Taiwan and the Penghu Islands; surrendered to the Qing 1683.

polities.name: Qing Taiwan
polities.note: Qing administration; effective control limited to the western plains (and Yilan from 1812) behind the 'aboriginal boundary' (tusiu line) until the 'open the mountains' policy of 1875; province 1885 with capital at Taipei; ceded to Japan 1895.

polities.name: Republic of Formosa
polities.note: Short-lived resistance state May–October 1895 against the Japanese takeover.

polities.name: Siraya
polities.note: Village-federations of the Tainan plains (Sinkan, Soulang, Mattau, Bakloan); under Dutch, Zheng and Qing rule from 1624 and largely assimilated by the 18th century.

polities.name: Ketagalan and Basay
polities.note: Plains peoples of the Taipei basin and north coast; largely displaced by Han settlement in the 18th century.

polities.name: Kavalan
polities.note: Some 36 villages of the Yilan (Lanyang) plain, outside Qing rule until Kavalan subprefecture was created 1812; later displaced southwards to Hualien.

polities.name: Atayal
polities.note: Mountain people of northern Taiwan, autonomous of Qing rule; subdued by Japanese campaigns 1900–1914.

polities.name: Seediq and Truku
polities.note: Mountain peoples of the central range around Wushe and the Taroko gorge; autonomous until the Japanese Truku War 1914.

polities.name: Bunun
polities.note: Mountain people of the central range, expanding south and east in the 18th–19th centuries; autonomous until Japanese rule.

polities.name: Tsou
polities.note: Alishan mountain people organised in large federated villages (hosa).

polities.name: Rukai
polities.note: Hereditary-chief villages of the southern central range.

polities.name: Paiwan
polities.note: Hereditary chiefdoms of southern Taiwan; the Tjuaqau (Langkiau) confederacy of the Hengchun peninsula under Tauketok dealt with the US after the Rover incident 1867; Mudan incident 1874 led to Japan's punitive expedition.

polities.name: Puyuma
polities.note: Puyuma chiefs held a paramountcy over the southeast coast plain (recognised by the Dutch and Qing as 'king of the south-east').

polities.name: Amis
polities.note: Largest indigenous people, of the east coast and Huatung rift valley; under Puyuma paramountcy in the south.

polities.name: Tao (Yami)
polities.note: Inhabitants of Orchid Island; no external rule until Japanese administration.

polities.name: Li lands of Hainan
polities.note: Interior highlands of Hainan held by the 'raw' Li under their own headmen (some as Ming/Qing tusi) while the coastal lowlands were Chinese Qiongzhou prefecture; repeated Li revolts; Qing campaigns opened the interior in the 1880s.

polities.name: Jianzhou Jurchens
polities.note: Ming-recognised Jurchen guard; Möngke Temür's Odoli at Hoeryong on the Tumen until 1433; resettled on the Suksu/Hun river north of the Yalu from the 1440s. Nurhaci unified it 1583–88 (Fe Ala 1587, Hetu Ala 1603) and proclaimed the Later Jin 1616.

polities.name: Hada
polities.note: Haixi Jurchen tribe controlling trade through the Guangshun pass at Kaiyuan; under Wang-tai (d.1582) led the Hūlun alliance; absorbed by Nurhaci 1601. Seat coordinates approximate.

polities.name: Ula
polities.note: Haixi Jurchen tribe on the upper Sungari north of modern Jilin city; Bujantai defeated and Ula absorbed by Nurhaci 1613.

polities.name: Hoifa
polities.note: Haixi Jurchen tribe on the Huifa river; destroyed by Nurhaci 1607.

polities.name: Yehe
polities.note: Strongest Haixi Jurchen tribe, allied with the Ming; last of the Hūlun to fall to Nurhaci (1619).

polities.name: Wild Jurchens
polities.note: Scattered Jurchen groups of eastern Manchuria (Mudan, Ussuri, Suifen, coast); brought under the Later Jin/Qing by raids and resettlement 1599–1640.

polities.name: Later Jin
polities.note: Nurhaci's Jurchen (Manchu) state; took Liaodong 1621; renamed Qing 1636.

polities.name: Nurgan Regional Military Commission (Ming)
polities.note: Ming outpost on the lower Amur supervising tributary guards of the Amur peoples; abandoned 1435. Nominal suzerainty only; draw beneath the native peoples.

polities.name: Nivkh
polities.note: Clan-based people of the Amur estuary and northern Sakhalin; tributary to Ming and Qing (Santan trade); under Russia after the Treaty of Aigun/Peking 1858–60.

polities.name: Ulch
polities.note: Lower Amur people central to the Santan trade between Qing and Sakhalin/Ezo.

polities.name: Nanai
polities.note: Fishing people of the middle Amur, lower Sungari and Ussuri; Qing tributaries via Sanxing; mostly under Russia after 1858–60 (Hezhe remained in Qing).

polities.name: Udege and Oroch
polities.note: Forest hunters of the Sikhote-Alin and Tatar Strait coast; nominal Qing tributaries until the Russian annexation of Primorye 1860.

polities.name: Duchers
polities.note: Agricultural people of the Amur between the Sungari and Ussuri described by Khabarov's and Stepanov's Cossacks; resettled by the Qing after 1658.

polities.name: Daur
polities.note: Fortified-village Mongolic farmers of the upper Amur and Zeya (princes Lavkai, Bombogor); tributary to the Later Jin/Qing from the 1630s; resettled south to the Nonni (Nen) valley by the Qing after Russian incursions 1650s.

polities.name: Solon Evenks
polities.note: Evenk and Daur clans of the Zeya–Amur forests; Bombogor's revolt against the Qing 1639–40; afterwards Qing banner tributaries.

polities.name: Hawaiʻi Island chiefdom
polities.note: Paramount chiefdom (aliʻi nui) of the island of Hawaiʻi, unified under ʻUmi-a-Līloa (c.1500) and again by Keawe and Alapaʻinui; Kamehameha I reunified it 1782–1791 and conquered Maui and Oʻahu 1795. Seat moved among Waipiʻo, Kona and Hilo.

polities.name: Maui chiefdom
polities.note: Paramount chiefdom of Maui with Lānaʻi and Kahoʻolawe (and Molokaʻi at times); under Kahekili II (r.1766–94) conquered Oʻahu 1783 and dominated Kauaʻi; fell to Kamehameha 1790/1795. Earlier seat at Hāna.

polities.name: Molokaʻi chiefdom
polities.note: Island chiefdom often subject to Oʻahu or Maui paramounts.

polities.name: Oʻahu chiefdom
polities.note: Paramount chiefdom of Oʻahu (Kākuhihewa, Kūaliʻi, Peleiōhōlani); conquered by Kahekili II of Maui 1783.

polities.name: Kauaʻi chiefdom
polities.note: Independent paramountcy of Kauaʻi and Niʻihau; Kaumualiʻi accepted Kamehameha I as overlord 1810 and was removed to Oʻahu 1821.

polities.name: Kingdom of Hawaii
polities.note: Founded by Kamehameha I's conquests 1795; Kauaʻi joined 1810. Seats Kailua-Kona (1812–20), Lahaina (1820–45), Honolulu (1845–93). Overthrown January 1893.

polities.name: Republic of Hawaii
polities.note: Provisional Government 1893–94 then Republic 1894–98; annexed by the United States August 1898.

polities.name: Tuʻi Tonga Empire
polities.note: Sacred paramountcy of Tonga; at its height (12th–15th c.) exacted tribute from Uvea, Futuna, parts of Samoa and Lau. From the 15th–17th c. temporal power passed to the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua and then Tuʻi Kanokupolu; the line ended 1865. Extent = Tonga archipelago (sphere wider before c.1500).

polities.name: Tuʻi Kanokupolu
polities.note: Executive kingship of Tonga from c.1610; its authority collapsed during the civil wars from 1799; Tāufaʻāhau (George Tupou I) took the title 1845 and founded the modern kingdom.

polities.name: Vavaʻu chiefdom
polities.note: Independent under the Finau ʻUlukālala chiefs during the Tongan civil wars; passed to Tāufaʻāhau 1833.

polities.name: Haʻapai chiefdom
polities.note: Haʻapai group; Tāufaʻāhau's power base from 1820 before his unification of Tonga 1845.

polities.name: Kingdom of Tonga
polities.note: Unified by George Tupou I (1845); constitution 1875; British protectorate 1900–70.

polities.name: Tui Manuʻa
polities.note: Ancient sacred paramountcy of the Manuʻa Islands (Taʻū, Ofu, Olosega); ceded to the United States 1904.

polities.name: Aʻana
polities.note: Western Upolu district polity whose paramount title Tuiaʻana is one of the four papa of the Tafaʻifā kingship.

polities.name: Atua
polities.note: Eastern Upolu district polity (Tuiatua title, Tumua seat Lufilufi).

polities.name: Tuamasaga (Malietoa)
polities.note: Central Upolu district, seat of the Malietoa title; Malietoa Vainuʻupō accepted Christianity 1830 and the Malietoa line was later recognised as kings of Samoa.

polities.name: Savaiʻi
polities.note: Savaiʻi's district centres (Safotulafai, Saleaula etc., the Pule orators) allied variously with Upolu factions.

polities.name: Tutuila
polities.note: Tutuila (with Aunuʻu), loosely attached to the Upolu Atua/Tuamasaga polities; ceded to the US 1900.

polities.name: Kingdom of Samoa
polities.note: Western-recognised Samoan government under Malietoa Laupepa and rivals (Tamasese, Mataʻafa) amid civil wars 1886–94 and 1898–99; partitioned between Germany and the US 1899–1900.

polities.name: Bau (Kubuna)
polities.note: Bauan state led by the Vunivalu; rose under Banuve and Naulivou (late 18th c., muskets from 1808) to dominate eastern Viti Levu, Lomaiviti and Ra; Cakobau claimed 'Tui Viti' and led the Kingdom of Fiji 1871; ceded Fiji to Britain 1874.

polities.name: Verata
polities.note: Senior eastern Viti Levu chiefdom eclipsed and sacked by Bau around 1800.

polities.name: Rewa (Burebasaga)
polities.note: Chiefdom of the Rewa delta under the Roko Tui Dreketi with Kadavu, Beqa, Namosi and Serua; Bau's main rival (war 1843–55).

polities.name: Cakaudrove
polities.note: Chiefdom of the Tui Cakau over southeastern Vanua Levu and Taveuni (with Natewa); later part of Maʻafu's Tovata. Extent drawn west of the 180° meridian only (Taveuni straddles it).

polities.name: Macuata
polities.note: Chiefdom of northeastern Vanua Levu.

polities.name: Lau (Tui Nayau)
polities.note: Eastern Fijian islands under the Tui Nayau of Lakeba, strongly linked with Tonga; the Tongan prince Enele Maʻafu became Tui Lau 1869.

polities.name: Tovata Confederacy
polities.note: Union of Lau, Cakaudrove, Bua and Macuata under Maʻafu; merged into the Kingdom of Fiji 1871. Area crosses the 180° meridian, so given as a radius.

polities.name: Western Viti Levu chiefdoms
polities.note: Independent chiefdoms of the dry western side of Viti Levu (Vuda, Ba, Nadi, Nadroga), outside the eastern confederacies.

polities.name: Kai Colo (Viti Levu highlands)
polities.note: Autonomous interior hill peoples of Viti Levu; resisted Cakobau's government and the colony (Colo wars 1873, 1876).

polities.name: Kingdom of Fiji
polities.note: Short-lived unified monarchy under Cakobau; ceded to Britain 10 October 1874. Area crosses 180°.

polities.name: Colony of Fiji
polities.note: British crown colony; Rotuma added 1881. Area crosses 180°.

polities.name: Rotuma
polities.note: Seven district chiefdoms of Rotuma; ceded to Britain 1881 (attached to Fiji).

polities.name: ʻUvea (Wallis)
polities.note: Kingdom of the Lavelua on Wallis Island, long tributary to the Tuʻi Tonga; French protectorate 1887.

polities.name: Futuna (Sigave and Alo)
polities.note: Two rival kingdoms (Sigave, Alo) on Futuna and Alofi; French protectorate 1888.

polities.name: Niue
polities.note: Island with elected kings (patu-iki) from c.1700 and the rival Motu/Tafiti moieties; British protectorate 1900, NZ 1901.

polities.name: Teva (southern Tahiti)
polities.note: Teva clan chiefdoms of south and southwest Tahiti Nui; under Purea and Amo seen by Wallis and Cook as the leading Tahitian house (1767–68); eclipsed by the Pōmare.

polities.name: Porionuʻu (Pare-Arue)
polities.note: Northwestern Tahiti chiefdom of Tu (Pōmare I) from which the Kingdom of Tahiti grew.

polities.name: Taiarapu (Tahiti Iti)
polities.note: Chiefdom of the Taiarapu peninsula under the Vehiatua line; defeated Teva/Purea 1768.

polities.name: Kingdom of Tahiti
polities.note: Created by Pōmare I and II; unified Tahiti and Moorea after Te Feipī 1815; nominal sway over the Tuamotus and some Austral Islands; French protectorate 1842, annexed 1880.

polities.name: Raiatea (Tamatoa)
polities.note: Sacred centre of the Society Islands under the Tamatoa line; conquered by Bora Bora's Puni c.1760s; restored kingdom 19th c.; annexed by France 1888 (resistance to 1897).

polities.name: Huahine
polities.note: Independent kingdom of Huahine (recognised by the Jarnac Convention 1847); French annexation completed 1895.

polities.name: Bora Bora
polities.note: Warrior chiefdom; under Puni conquered Raiatea, Tahaʻa and Maupiti (1760s); independent kingdom until French annexation 1888.

polities.name: Mangareva
polities.note: Kingdom of the Gambier Islands (ʻAkariki); French protectorate 1844, annexed 1881.

polities.name: Tuamotu chiefdoms
polities.note: Atoll chiefdoms; the Anaa (Parata) warriors dominated the western atolls before Pōmare overlordship (1820s) and French rule.

polities.name: Austral Islands chiefdoms
polities.note: Separate island chiefdoms/kingdoms; Tubuai and Raivavae under Pōmare influence, annexed by France 1880–1900.

polities.name: Northern Marquesas tribes
polities.note: Valley tribes (mata ʻeinaʻa) of Nuku Hiva, Ua Pou and Ua Huka under hereditary haka'iki; no island-wide ruler; annexed by France 1842.

polities.name: Southern Marquesas tribes
polities.note: Valley tribes of Hiva Oa, Tahuata and Fatu Hiva (Iotete of Tahuata ceded to France 1842).

polities.name: Rarotonga (ariki)
polities.note: Three tribal districts (Te Au o Tonga under Makea, Takitumu under Pa and Kainuku, Puaikura); British protectorate 1888 and Cook Islands Federation 1891 under Makea Takau; annexed by NZ 1901.

polities.name: Aitutaki
polities.note: Ariki of Aitutaki; British protectorate 1888.

polities.name: Mangaia
polities.note: Island polity ruled by the war-winning 'Temporal Lord of Mangaia' (Mangaia) and the Ngariki priestly ariki.

polities.name: Ko Tuʻu Aro (Miru and western Rapa Nui)
polities.note: Western/northern confederation of Rapa Nui clans led by the Miru, whose ariki mau was paramount of the island; island depopulated by Peruvian slave raids 1862–63; annexed by Chile 1888.

polities.name: Hotu Iti (eastern Rapa Nui)
polities.note: Eastern confederation of Rapa Nui clans (Tupahotu, Koro Orongo etc.), rival of Ko Tuʻu Aro.

polities.name: Muriwhenua iwi
polities.note: Far North iwi of the Aupōuri peninsula, Kaitaia and Doubtless Bay.

polities.name: Ngāpuhi
polities.note: Largest iwi, of the Bay of Islands and Hokianga; under Hongi Hika led musket-armed raids across the North Island 1818–1823 (Musket Wars); signatories of the 1835 Declaration and 1840 Treaty; Northern War 1845–46.

polities.name: Ngāti Whātua
polities.note: Iwi of the Kaipara and Tāmaki isthmus (conquered Tāmaki from Waiohua c.1740); sold/gifted the site of Auckland 1840.

polities.name: Hauraki iwi (Marutūahu)
polities.note: Marutūahu confederation of the Hauraki Gulf, Coromandel and Hauraki plains.

polities.name: Waikato-Tainui
polities.note: Tainui iwi of the Waikato basin (Ngāti Mahuta, Ngāti Hauā etc.); core of the Kīngitanga from 1858; lands confiscated after the 1863–64 Waikato invasion, when the King moved to the King Country.

polities.name: Kīngitanga (Māori King Movement)
polities.note: Pan-tribal monarchy (Pōtatau Te Wherowhero 1858, Tāwhiao 1860) to halt land sales, centred on Waikato with Ngāti Maniapoto, Ngāti Hauā and allies. After the 1863–64 war the 'King Country' (Rohe Pōtae) was closed to Europeans until Tāwhiao's reconciliation 1881 and the opening of the main trunk survey 1883–85.

polities.name: Ngāti Maniapoto
polities.note: Tainui iwi of the Waipā headwaters and the King Country (Rohe Pōtae).

polities.name: Ngāti Toa
polities.note: Tainui iwi of Kāwhia; driven out by Waikato 1821, migrated under Te Rauparaha to Kapiti and Porirua (Te Heke) and conquered the Kāpiti coast and the northern South Island (Wairau, Nelson, Kaikōura raids) 1820s–1830s; Wairau affray 1843.

polities.name: Ngāti Raukawa
polities.note: Tainui iwi of the upper Waikato (Maungatautari); a large part migrated to Ōtaki and the Manawatū–Horowhenua coast with Ngāti Toa 1820s.

polities.name: Te Āti Awa
polities.note: Iwi of north Taranaki; many migrated south 1820s–30s to Wellington harbour (Te Whanganui-a-Tara) and Queen Charlotte Sound; Waitara purchase dispute began the First Taranaki War 1860.

polities.name: Ngāti Mutunga and Ngāti Tama
polities.note: North Taranaki iwi; migrated to Wellington and invaded the Chatham Islands 1835, subjugating the Moriori until c.1863.

polities.name: Taranaki and south Taranaki iwi
polities.note: Taranaki, Ngāruahine, Ngāti Ruanui and Ngā Rauru around the mountain and south Taranaki bight; Titokowaru's war 1868–69; Parihaka passive resistance 1866–81.

polities.name: Whanganui iwi
polities.note: River iwi of the Whanganui.

polities.name: Ngāti Tūwharetoa
polities.note: Iwi of Lake Taupō and the central volcanic plateau under the Te Heuheu paramount chiefs.

polities.name: Te Arawa
polities.note: Confederation of iwi of the Rotorua lakes and Maketu coast; mostly allied with the Crown in the 1860s.

polities.name: Ngāi Te Rangi
polities.note: Iwi of Tauranga harbour (with Ngāti Ranginui and Ngāti Pūkenga); Gate Pā 1864.

polities.name: Ngāti Awa
polities.note: Iwi of the Rangitāiki plains and Whakatāne.

polities.name: Ngāi Tūhoe
polities.note: Mountain iwi of Te Urewera; sheltered Te Kooti 1869–72; Urewera largely autonomous until the 1890s.

polities.name: Te Whānau-ā-Apanui
polities.note: Iwi of the eastern Bay of Plenty coast between Ōpōtiki and Pōtikirua.

polities.name: Ngāti Porou
polities.note: Iwi of the East Cape (Tairāwhiti north of Gisborne).

polities.name: Tūranga iwi
polities.note: Iwi of Poverty Bay (Tūranga); Te Kooti's base and the 1868 Matawhero attack.

polities.name: Ngāti Kahungunu
polities.note: Iwi of Hawke's Bay and the Wairarapa (Wairoa to Cape Palliser).

polities.name: Rangitāne and Muaūpoko
polities.note: Kurahaupō iwi of the Manawatū, Horowhenua and Rangitīkei; partly displaced by Ngāti Toa and Ngāti Raukawa in the 1820s.

polities.name: Te Tau Ihu Kurahaupō iwi
aliases: Ngāti Apa ki te Rā Tō
polities.note: Iwi of the northern South Island (Nelson, Marlborough Sounds, Wairau, Golden Bay) until conquest by Ngāti Toa, Te Āti Awa and allies 1828–1830.

polities.name: Ngāti Māmoe
polities.note: Earlier South Island iwi (absorbing Waitaha), progressively conquered and intermarried by migrating Ngāi Tahu from the 1600s; remnants in Fiordland into the 18th century.

polities.name: Ngāi Tahu
polities.note: Iwi that migrated from the east coast North Island to the South Island in the 17th century, absorbing Waitaha and Ngāti Māmoe; held most of Te Waipounamu south of Kaikōura incl. Westland (pounamu); Kaiapoi sacked by Ngāti Toa 1832; land sold to the Crown 1844–64.

polities.name: Moriori
polities.note: Pacifist Polynesian people of the Chatham Islands (Rēkohu); invaded and enslaved by Ngāti Mutunga and Ngāti Tama 1835.

polities.name: United Tribes of New Zealand
polities.note: Confederation of northern chiefs (mostly Ngāpuhi and allies) declaring independence 1835; superseded by the Treaty of Waitangi 1840. Umbrella over the northern iwi entries.

polities.name: Colony of New Zealand
polities.note: British colony after the Treaty of Waitangi (1840); effective control limited to settler districts until the 1870s–80s (King Country, Urewera remained autonomous). Draw beneath the iwi entries.

polities.name: Eora and Darug
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Sydney basin peoples; first to face British colonisation 1788 (Pemulwuy's resistance 1790–1802).

polities.name: Hunter and Central Coast nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Hunter Valley and Port Stephens peoples.

polities.name: Mid-North Coast nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Coastal nations between the Clarence and the Manning.

polities.name: Bundjalung and Northern Rivers
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Bundjalung confederation of the far north coast of NSW and Gold Coast hinterland.

polities.name: Gamilaraay and northwestern slopes
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Gamilaraay and neighbours of the Liverpool Plains and Namoi–Gwydir; Myall Creek massacre 1838.

polities.name: Wiradjuri
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Largest nation of NSW (Lachlan, Macquarie, Murrumbidgee); Bathurst war 1824 (Windradyne).

polities.name: Yuin, Ngunnawal and Monaro nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. South coast, Canberra region and Monaro tablelands.

polities.name: Barkindji and Darling basin
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Darling river peoples and the dry western plains of NSW.

polities.name: Yorta Yorta and Murray riverine nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Murray river nations of northern Victoria.

polities.name: Kulin nation
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Alliance of five language groups around Port Phillip; Batman 'treaty' 1835.

polities.name: Gunditjmara and Western District nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Western Victoria; Gunditjmara eel-trap settlements; Eumeralla wars 1840s.

polities.name: Gunaikurnai
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Gippsland nation of five clans.

polities.name: Ngarrindjeri
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Confederation of lakes and Coorong clans under the Tendi council.

polities.name: Kaurna and Gulf nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Adelaide plains and Yorke Peninsula.

polities.name: Adnyamathanha and Eyre Peninsula nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Flinders Ranges and Eyre Peninsula.

polities.name: Lake Eyre basin nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Channel Country and Lake Eyre basin; Cooper Creek trade networks.

polities.name: Western Desert peoples
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Very large bloc of closely related desert dialect groups; little colonial contact before the 20th century.

polities.name: Nullarbor and Goldfields nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Nullarbor coast and the eastern Goldfields of WA.

polities.name: Arrernte
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Central Australian nation of the MacDonnell Ranges; Hermannsburg mission 1877.

polities.name: Warlpiri and Tanami nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Tanami desert and Tennant Creek region.

polities.name: Yolŋu
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Northeast Arnhem Land clans; long contact with Makassan trepangers (c.1720–1906).

polities.name: Western Arnhem Land nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Kakadu–western Arnhem escarpment and Cobourg peninsula peoples.

polities.name: Larrakia and Top End west nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Darwin region, Daly River and Katherine.

polities.name: Tiwi
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Bathurst and Melville islands; resisted the British Fort Dundas 1824–29.

polities.name: Victoria River and Barkly nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Victoria River district and Barkly Tableland.

polities.name: Gulf Country nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Southern Gulf of Carpentaria coast and Wellesley Islands.

polities.name: Kalkadoon and northwest Queensland nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Kalkadoon resistance ended at Battle Mountain 1884.

polities.name: Cape York nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Cape York peninsula and the Wet Tropics rainforest.

polities.name: Torres Strait Islanders
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Melanesian island communities; annexed to Queensland 1872–79.

polities.name: Central Queensland coast nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Burdekin to Burnett coast and hinterland.

polities.name: Southeast Queensland nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Brisbane, Moreton Bay and Sunshine Coast hinterland (Bunya gatherings).

polities.name: Southwest Queensland nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Warrego, Maranoa and upper Barcoo river nations.

polities.name: Noongar
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Fourteen dialect groups of southwest WA; Pinjarra massacre 1834.

polities.name: Yamatji nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Murchison and Gascoyne regions.

polities.name: Pilbara nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Pilbara coast and ranges; pearling labour coercion from the 1860s.

polities.name: Kimberley nations
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Kimberley; Jandamarra's Bunuba resistance 1894–97.

polities.name: Palawa (Aboriginal Tasmanians)
polities.note: Aboriginal nation region drawn at the scale of a cultural-linguistic bloc (many distinct nations/clans inside, no single ruler). Boundaries approximate, after the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia. Nine nations of Tasmania; devastated in the Black War (1824–31); survivors removed to Flinders Island (Wybalenna) 1833 and Oyster Cove 1847.

polities.name: Colony of New South Wales
polities.note: British penal then self-governing colony; settled area grew from the Cumberland Plain (1788–1813) across the Blue Mountains (1813) to the 'Nineteen Counties' (1829) and the squatting districts. Victoria (1851) and Queensland (1859) split off. Effective control drawn by phase; draw Aboriginal nations beneath/outside.

polities.name: Van Diemen's Land
polities.note: Settled 1803; separate colony 1825; renamed Tasmania 1856.

polities.name: Swan River Colony / Western Australia
polities.note: Founded 1829 (King George Sound outpost 1826); effective control long limited to the southwest, expanding north via pastoral and pearling frontiers.

polities.name: Province of South Australia
polities.note: Free colony founded 1836; administered the Northern Territory 1863–1911 (Palmerston/Darwin founded 1869). Effective settlement concentrated south of Port Augusta and along the Overland Telegraph (1872).

polities.name: Colony of Victoria
polities.note: Port Phillip District of NSW from 1836; separate colony 1851.

polities.name: Colony of Queensland
polities.note: Moreton Bay penal settlement 1824 (NSW); separate colony 1859; frontier (Native Police) advanced north and west through the 1860s–80s.

polities.name: Raja Ampat kingdoms
polities.note: Four petty kingdoms (rajas) of Waigeo, Salawati, Misool and Waigama under the Sultanate of Tidore; Dutch claims over 'Tidore's Papua' from 1660/1828, outposts only from 1898.

polities.name: Onin petty kingdoms (Fakfak)
polities.note: Coastal rajadoms of the Onin (Bomberai) peninsula linked to Seram and Tidore traders.

polities.name: Kaimana (Sran kingdom)
polities.note: Petty kingdom of Kaimana/Namatota on the south Bird's Head coast, tributary to Tidore.

polities.name: Biak-Numfor
polities.note: Seafaring raiders and traders of Biak and Numfor who settled the Raja Ampat and Bird's Head coasts and paid tribute to Tidore.

polities.name: Sentani and Humboldt Bay chiefdoms
polities.note: Hereditary ondoafi chiefdoms around Lake Sentani and Humboldt Bay.

polities.name: Asmat
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Swamp-forest headhunting villages of the southwest coast.

polities.name: Marind-anim
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Large headhunting people of the south New Guinea plain.

polities.name: Dani (Baliem Valley)
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Dense highland agricultural population with warring confederacies; unknown to outsiders until 1938.

polities.name: Mee (Ekari) highlands
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Western highlands around the Paniai (Wissel) lakes.

polities.name: Motu-Koitabu
polities.note: Motu pottery villages and Koita around Port Moresby, organising the hiri trading voyages to the Gulf of Papua.

polities.name: Kiwai (Fly delta)
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Peoples of the Fly River estuary.

polities.name: Trobriand chiefdoms
polities.note: Ranked chiefdoms of Kiriwina (Tabalu paramount at Omarakana) within the kula exchange ring of the Massim islands.

polities.name: Orokaiva
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Peoples of the Oro (Northern) plains.

polities.name: Madang and Siassi trading peoples
polities.note: Bilbil potters of Astrolabe Bay and Siassi sea traders linking New Guinea and New Britain; Miklouho-Maclay 1871–72.

polities.name: Iatmul (Middle Sepik)
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Large river villages of the middle Sepik.

polities.name: Abelam (Maprik)
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Prince Alexander foothills yam-cult villages.

polities.name: Enga
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Western highland people; Tee exchange system.

polities.name: Huli
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Southern highlands people of the Tari basin.

polities.name: Melpa (Mount Hagen)
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Wahgi valley people; Moka exchange.

polities.name: Simbu (Chimbu)
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Dense highland population of the Chimbu valley.

polities.name: Eastern Highlands peoples
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land.

polities.name: Tolai (Gazelle Peninsula)
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Shell-money (tabu) societies of the Gazelle peninsula, New Britain; German Herbertshöhe 1899.

polities.name: New Ireland (Malagan societies)
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land.

polities.name: Manus (Admiralty Islands)
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Titan sea-traders and Usiai inland villages.

polities.name: Bougainville and Buka
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land.

polities.name: German New Guinea
polities.note: German protectorate (Neuguinea-Kompagnie to 1899) over northeastern New Guinea, the Bismarck Archipelago and northern Solomons; effective control coastal only. Seats Finschhafen 1885–91, Madang 1891–99, Herbertshöhe 1899–1910.

polities.name: British New Guinea
polities.note: British protectorate 1884, colony 1888; transferred to Australia 1906. Effective control coastal.

polities.name: Roviana
polities.note: Headhunting chiefdom of the New Georgia group (19th-c. paramount chiefs Ingova, Hingava).

polities.name: Santa Isabel (Bughotu)
polities.note: Bughotu chiefs (Soga, 1880s) of southern Santa Isabel.

polities.name: Choiseul
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land.

polities.name: Malaita
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Densely settled; artificial-island sea peoples (Lau, Langa Langa) and bush peoples.

polities.name: Guadalcanal peoples
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land.

polities.name: Makira (San Cristobal)
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land.

polities.name: British Solomon Islands Protectorate
polities.note: British protectorate over the southern Solomons from 1893 (Tulagi 1896); northern islands added 1899–1900.

polities.name: Tanna
polities.note: District alliances (Koiameta/Numrukwen moieties) of Tanna.

polities.name: Southern Vanuatu islands
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land.

polities.name: Efate and Shepherd chiefdoms
polities.note: Chiefly (naveika) societies of Efate and the Shepherds.

polities.name: Malakula
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Graded societies of Malakula.

polities.name: Espiritu Santo
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land.

polities.name: Central-north Vanuatu (Ambae, Pentecost, Maewo, Ambrym)
polities.note: Stateless lineage/village society (big-man or clan leadership, no paramount ruler); drawn as a cultural-linguistic area so the atlas can fill the land. Graded-society (nimangki/sumbwe) islands.

polities.name: Anglo-French Condominium (New Hebrides)
polities.note: Joint Naval Commission 1887, Condominium 1906; effective control only around mission and plantation stations before 1900.

polities.name: Hoot ma Waap chiefdoms
polities.note: Kanak chiefdoms of the far north (Hienghène of Bouarate, Pouébo, Koumac).

polities.name: Paicî-Cèmuhî chiefdoms
polities.note: Central-northern Kanak chiefdoms.

polities.name: Ajië-Arhö chiefdoms
polities.note: Central Kanak chiefdoms; centre of Ataï's 1878 revolt (La Foa).

polities.name: Southern Kanak chiefdoms (Xârâcùù and Drubea-Kapumë)
polities.note: Southern Kanak chiefdoms around Canala, Thio and the Nouméa region.

polities.name: Loyalty Islands chiefdoms
polities.note: Paramount chiefdoms (grandes chefferies) of Lifou, Maré and Ouvéa; annexed by France 1864.

polities.name: French New Caledonia
polities.note: French colony from 1853 (penal colony 1864–97); Kanak lands confined to reserves after the 1878 revolt. Draw Kanak chiefdoms on top before c.1880.

polities.name: Yap (and Sawei sphere)
polities.note: Village hierarchies of Yap; Gagil district was overlord of the outer Carolinian atolls (Ulithi to Namonuito) through the sawei tribute system. Spanish 1886, German 1899.

polities.name: Palau – Koror (Ibedul)
polities.note: Southern Palauan federation led by the Ibedul of Koror; rival of Melekeok; Spanish 1885, German 1899.

polities.name: Palau – Melekeok (Reklai)
polities.note: Northern Palauan federation led by the Reklai of Melekeok (Babeldaob).

polities.name: Saudeleur dynasty
polities.note: Centralised dynasty ruling Pohnpei from the megalithic capital Nan Madol; overthrown by Isokelekel c.1628.

polities.name: Pohnpei chiefdoms (Nahnmwarki)
polities.note: Five paramount chiefdoms (wehi) under Nahnmwarki and Nahnken titles after the Saudeleur; Spanish 1886, German 1899 (Sokehs rebellion 1910).

polities.name: Kosrae (Tokosa)
polities.note: Island-wide kingdom under the Tokosa at Lelu, with stone-walled capital; collapsed after depopulation and conversion in the 1870s.

polities.name: Chamorro chiefdoms (Mariana Islands)
polities.note: Village chiefdoms led by maga'låhi across Guam and the Marianas; Spanish mission 1668; Spanish–Chamorro wars 1670–1695 ended independence and the northern islanders were concentrated on Guam.

polities.name: Spanish Mariana Islands
polities.note: Spanish colony under the Philippines; Guam ceded to the US 1898, rest sold to Germany 1899.

polities.name: Ralik Chain (Marshall Islands)
polities.note: Western Marshall chain under iroijlaplap paramount chiefs (Kabua, Loeak); German protectorate 1885.

polities.name: Ratak Chain (Marshall Islands)
polities.note: Eastern Marshall chain under rival iroij; German protectorate 1885.

polities.name: Abemama kingdom
polities.note: Central Gilberts kingdom built by Tem Baiteke and his son Tem Binoka (r.1878–91) over Abemama, Aranuka and Kuria; British protectorate 1892.

polities.name: Butaritari–Makin high chiefdom
polities.note: Hereditary high chiefs (uea) of Butaritari and Makin; British protectorate 1892.

gaps.area: Interior of Primorye / Sikhote-Alin and upper Ussuri forests
gaps.note: Very sparse Udege/Nanai hunting bands; polygons above are indicative only.

gaps.area: Northern Sakhalin interior and Okhotsk coast north of the Amur
gaps.note: Sparse Nivkh, Uilta (Orok) and Evenk bands with no recognised seat; Okhotsk coast falls to Russian Siberia after 1640s (other region).
Atoll communities under island-level ulu/aliki councils; no multi-island polity. British protectorate 1892.
Three atolls; Fakaofo held loose hegemony over Atafu and Nukunonu in the 18th–19th c. British protectorate 1889. Too small to draw.

gaps.area: Pitcairn, Henderson and the Line/Phoenix Islands
gaps.note: Uninhabited for most of the period (Pitcairn settled by Bounty mutineers 1790).

gaps.area: Southern Alps, Fiordland interior and Southland high country (South Island)
gaps.note: Mountain land with seasonal use only (pounamu trails); claimed within Ngāi Tahu / Ngāti Māmoe rohe but no settlement.

gaps.area: Central North Island ranges (Kaimanawa, Ruahine) and Rangitaiki plateau
gaps.note: Sparsely used uplands between Tūwharetoa, Tūhoe, Kahungunu and Whanganui rohe.

gaps.area: Simpson Desert and Great Sandy/Gibson Desert interiors
gaps.note: Within Western Desert / Lake Eyre bloc lands but very thinly occupied; no seats. Aboriginal regions above are cultural blocs, not states.
Colonial control limited to Palmerston (Darwin), the Overland Telegraph line and pastoral leases; Aboriginal nations governed most land.

gaps.area: Lowland and foothill rainforest of interior New Guinea (Mamberamo basin, upper Fly, Strickland, Purari, Ramu interiors)
gaps.note: Hundreds of small autonomous language/clan groups with no recognised seats or supra-village polities; scattered entries above sample only the best-documented peoples. Much of west New Guinea's south coast (Kamoro/Mimika) and the Bird's Head interior likewise.

gaps.area: New Britain (outside the Gazelle) and the Huon Peninsula
gaps.note: Small autonomous village societies (Kilenge, Arawe, Baining, Jabem); no polities.

gaps.area: Chuuk (Truk) lagoon and the central Carolinian atolls
gaps.note: Clan-based island communities without island-wide chiefs; outer atolls were within Yap's sawei network.
Nauru's twelve clans and southern Gilbertese councils (mwaneaba) had no central ruler; Nauru German 1888, Gilberts British 1892.

gaps.area: Santa Cruz Islands, Rennell-Bellona, Ontong Java and the Polynesian outliers
gaps.note: Small island communities, below map scale.
